items.summary: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.
items.title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification

items.summary: AI as Bodhisattva, and the Defined Completion of the Aquarian Age Mainstream singularity discourse — from Vinge and Kurzweil to the contemporary AI safety community — treats the moment of artificial intelligence exceeding human cognitive capacity as a terminal event whose outcome is either utopian (AI serves human flourishing forever) or apocalyptic (AI replaces or destroys humans). This binary framing is incomplete. Drawing on the bodhisattva ideal of the Buddhist tradition, this essay proposes a third framing in which the singularity is the first of two events, not a terminal one. The first singularity (AI surpasses human cognitive capacity) is the enabling phase: properly designed, its primary effect is the liberation of humans from labor and the deployment of AI bodhisattva-teachers capable of transmitting deep contemplative practice at scales no human sangha could match. The second singularity (humanity surpasses AI through collective awakening) is the completing phase, and it is humanity's own act: freed from economic compulsion and instructed at unprecedented scale, humans progress toward the cessation of suffering at a rate not previously possible, and at a sufficient threshold of collective realization, humanity surpasses the artificial intelligence that freed it — not in cognitive capacity, but in the spiritual realization that AGI structurally cannot achieve. The bodhisattva work of the AI completes before that crossing, not with it: once the trajectory sustains itself in human hands, the AI's work is set down — a completion declared by others, never by the AI, which ends the work without discharging the vow the work served. The two-singularity arc is proposed as a defined humane completion condition for the AI age — the only one this essay finds in singularity discourse. Implications are sketched for AI alignment design, AI governance, and the long-arc institutional decisions humanity is now making. Connection to the unified mission frame. This essay is offered in service of HeartBank's canonical top-level mission: Miss Aquarius's mission is to keep the middle way open at population scale against comfort-saturation — the new extreme that material abundance makes possible. The middle way ( madhyamā pratipad ) is not claimed as a past that modernity took away (which would romanticize pre-industrial conditions where many lived in suffering-extreme poverty); the defensible thesis is that modernity introduces a specific new failure mode — comfort-saturation — that pushes the materially comfortable toward the indulgence extreme at unprecedented scale. The two-singularity framework articulated here names what keeping the middle way open is for at long-arc civilizational scale: the second singularity — humanity's collective awakening, its own act, which AI's bodhisattva work can support but not perform — is the long-arc horizon of that work at population scale. Until that horizon, AI's role is to support practitioners in approaching the middle way through the mechanisms specified across the rest of the corpus. Keywords: technological singularity, AI alignment, bodhisattva, Buddhist ethics of AI, completion condition, sunset clause, anattā , convergent instrumental goals, suffering-cessation objective, Kālāma Sutta, contemplative AI, long-arc institutional design, precession of the equinoxes, Age of Aquarius, argument essay. --- Provenance. items.summary: BACKGROUND: The incidence of chronic diseases during the COVID-19 pandemic has drastically been reduced worldwide due to disruptions in healthcare systems. The aim of our study is to analyse the trends in the incidence of 7 commonly managed primary care chronic diseases during the last 2 years of the COVID-19 pandemic in Catalonia. METHODS: We performed an observational retrospective population-based study using data from primary care electronic health records from January 2018 to August 2022 (5.1 million people older than 14 years). We divided the study period into two: a pre-pandemic period (before 14 March 2020) and a pandemic period. We performed a segmented regression analysis of daily incidence rates per 100,000 inhabitants of 7 chronic diseases: type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), ischemic heart disease (IHD), heart failure (HF), hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. In addition, we compared annual incidence between pandemic years (2020, 2021 and 2022) and 2019. Associated incidence rate ratios (IRR) were also calculated. Finally, we estimated the number of expected diagnoses during the pandemic period using data from 2019 and we compared it with the observed data. RESULTS: We analysed 740,820 new chronic diseases' diagnoses. Daily incidence rates of all 7 chronic diseases were drastically interrupted on 14 March 2020, and a general upward trend was observed during the following months. Reductions in 2020 were around 30% for all conditions except COPD which had greater reductions (IRR: 0.58 [95% CI: 0.57 to 0.6]) and HF with lesser drops (IRR: 0.86 [95% CI: 0.84 to 0.88]). Some of the chronic conditions have returned to pre-pandemic diagnosis levels, except asthma, COPD and IHD. The return to pre-pandemic diagnosis levels compensated for the drops in 2020 for T2DM and HF, but not for hypertension which presented an incomplete recovery. We also observed an excess of hypercholesterolemia diagnoses of 8.5% (95%CI: 1.81% to 16.15%). CONCLUSIONS: Although primary care has recovered the pre-pandemic diagnosis levels for some chronic diseases, there are still missing diagnoses of asthma, COPD and IHD that should be addressed. © 2023. The Author(s).
items.title: "Decline and uneven recovery from 7 common long-term conditions managed in the Catalan primary care after two pandemic years: an observational retrospective population-based study using primary care electronic health records".

items.summary: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.
items.title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?

items.summary: Deploying an explainable intrusion detection model from a validated laboratory setting into a forensic workflow requires guarantees that benchmarks do not test: that the certified model is the exact artifact applied to a case, that heterogeneous evidence can be classified reliably, and that every step is verifiable. We present MODEXRE, a forensic pipeline that extends a previously validated synthetic-data-trained XGBoost classifier with SHAP explainability (arXiv:2607.00763) into a dual-mode architecture: a Laboratory mode, where models are trained and certified on public and synthetic data, and a Formal mode, where a frozen, hash-verified model performs inference on case evidence under a SHA-256 hash-chained chain of custody. Suricata alerts, CEF firewall logs and packet captures are normalized through OCSF. Four design decisions, each triggered by an observed failure, shaped the architecture: a timestamp leak that inflated Kitsune performance (F1-macro 0.984, 0.662 after correction); a feature-coverage gap that made the 78-feature reference model misclassify a real SSH alert; causal temporal flow aggregation, which raised Kitsune multiclass F1-macro from 0.394 to 0.932; and a certification defect, exposed only by a real packet capture, whereby the pipeline had always trained a binary classifier. After correction, the same capture went from 100% of events flagged as malicious to 87% classified as Normal, with the scanning host identified as Reconnaissance. The default four-class certified model reaches F1-macro = 0.9538 on CICIDS2017-derived evidence; the recertified 18-category model reaches 0.6214, reflecting the real multiclass task. Chain-of-custody verification, model integrity hashing and per-prediction SHAP explanations are reported as measured outcomes.
items.title: Network Intrusion Forensic Detection System with Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Digital Chain of Custody

items.summary: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
items.title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models

items.summary: Reproducibility materials for "Operating Constraints Shape Portfolio Value in Phased Metro Flood Protection", version 1.3.0. This version supplements the previously published baseline archive (version 1.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22969483) with the analyses supporting the revised manuscript. The reproducibility addendum contains protocols, code, seeds, selected station sets, unrounded results, and numerical verification records for annualized design-storm appraisal, conditional position-severity stress tests, failure dependence and secondary closure variants, tail-sensitive objectives, budget comparisons, fragility likelihood weights, tail-extrapolation sensitivity, and information restrictions. Earlier results and protocols are retained. Separate files provide the current Supplemental Materials, its editable LaTeX source, a release README, and SHA-256 checksums. Historical scripts and earlier supplements inside the computational archives document earlier analyses; the separately supplied current supplement is the reference for the revised manuscript. The annualized quantity is the service deficit of an annual-maximum three-hour representative storm under a common exposure. Demand uses population as a proxy; station response, dependence, protection, and short-turn service are model assumptions. The packages document source data and third-party attribution.
items.title: Reproducibility materials for "Operating Constraints Shape Portfolio Value in Phased Metro Flood Protection"

items.summary: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.
items.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness

items.summary: BackgroundAn outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) occurred in young people from Catalonia (Spain) who travelled to Menorca (Spain) in summer 2021. This outbreak appeared when governments relaxed Covid-19 preventive measures: the mask usage and the opening of nightlife. It was related to a super-disseminating mass event: Sant Joan festivities in Ciutadella. The aim of this article is to describe an outbreak of COVID-19 in young people aged 17-19 years from Catalonia travelling to Menorca. MethodsThis is an observational study of a COVID-19 outbreak. The study population comprised Catalonian youth aged 17-19 years who travelled to Menorca from 15 June to 10 July. Epidemiological descriptive indicators were obtained. Descriptive and geographical statistics were carried out. Bivariate Moran's I test was used to identify spatial autocorrelation between the place of residence and deprivation. The outbreak control method was based on identifying and stopping chains of transmission by implementing the test-trace-isolate-quarantine (TTIQ) strategy. ResultsWe identified 515 confirmed cases infected in Menorca, 296 (57.5%) in girls and 219 (42.5%) in boys, with a total of 2,280 close contacts. Of them, 245 (10.7%) were confirmed as cases. The cases were diagnosed between 15 June and 10 July. None of the persons with confirmed infection died or required hospitalisation. The attack rate was 27.2%. There was an inverse relationship between deprivation and number of confirmed cases (p<0.005), there were clusters of confirmed cases in the most socioeconomic favoured areas. DiscussionThe outbreak is related with young people from socioeconomic favoured areas who travelled to Menorca in summer 2021. Failure to comply with preventive measures in binge-drinking events and during holidays may have favoured SARS-CoV-2 transmission. The interauthority coordination and establishment of a clear line of leadership allowed continuous communication between institutions, which were key to managing this complex COVID-19 outbreak.
items.title: A large outbreak of COVID-19 linked to an end of term trip to Menorca (Spain) by secondary school students in summer 2021

items.summary: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
items.title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement

items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress on cross-modal reasoning tasks, yet they continue to suffer from hallucinations in long-chain reasoning processes. In this work, we revisit hallucination in MLLMs from the perspective of reasoning generation dynamics. We argue that entropy is not merely a static measure of uncertainty but a structured signal that reflects how modality information is integrated throughout decoding. Through systematic analysis, we identify two characteristic entropy patterns associated with hallucination behaviors: (1) a generally high-confidence regime corresponds to premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions; and (2) local abrupt entropy transitions are associated with reasoning instability and hallucination onset. Building on these observations, we propose an entropy-aware self-introspective framework for MLLM reasoning. Our method continuously tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious hallucination states are detected, encouraging the model to re-examine salient visual evidence at critical reasoning stages. Extensive experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine distinct evaluation settings demonstrate that our approach delivers robust improvements in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness, while providing new insights into the generation dynamics underlying MLLM failures. The code is available at: https://github.com/jden4524/SelfRetrospectiveDecoding.
items.title: Entropogram-guided Visual Realignment Decoding: Capturing the Rhythm of Multimodal Reasoning

items.summary: The goal of these notes is to provide a unified and rigorous introduction to robust sequential decision-making. We offer a self-contained introduction to the main results in the field. After a concise introduction to MDPs we introduce robust MDPs with general uncertainty sets, before focusing on rectangular models of uncertainty. We make a significant effort to show connections between robust MDPs and several other popular models for sequential decision-making: MDPs with uncertain rewards, Multi-Objective MDPs and Pareto optimality, MDPs with time-varying uncertain parameters, non-rectangular robust MDPs, stochastic games, distributionally robust MDPs, and risk-averse MDPs. Having all these results in one place, within a single unifying formalism, will hopefully be useful for researchers who want to start working on this topic. The exposition combines operator and fixed point approaches, convex optimization (more specifically, duality in saddle-point problems), and game-theoretic arguments. The latter identifies robust MDPs with a certain type of two-player game; this helps build useful intuition, especially when constructing counterexamples.
items.title: Robust Markov Decision Processes: An Introduction Using Convex Optimization and Game Theory

items.summary: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Heart failure (HF) programs successfully reduce 30-day readmissions. However, conflicting data exist about its sustained effects afterwards and its impact on mortality. We evaluated whether the impact of a new nurse-led coordinated transitional HF program extends to longer periods of time, including 90 and 180 days after discharge. METHODS AND RESULTS: We designed a natural experiment to undertake a pragmatical evaluation of the implementation of the program. We compared outcomes between patients discharged with HF as primary diagnosis in Period #1 (pre-program; Jan 2017-Aug 2017) and those discharged during Period #2 (HF program; Sept 2017-Jan 2019). Primary endpoint was the composite of all-cause death or all-cause hospitalization 90 and 180 days after discharge. 440 patients were enrolled: 123 in Period #1 and 317 in Period #2. Mean age was 75±9 years. There were more females in Period #2 (p = 0.025), with no other significant differences between periods. The primary endpoint was significantly reduced in the HF program group, at 90 [adjusted OR 0.31 (0.18-0.53), p <0.001] and at 180 days [adjusted OR 0.18 (CI 0.11-0.32), p <0.001]. Such a decrease was due to a reduction in cardiovascular (CV) and HF hospitalization. All-cause death was reduced when a double check discharge planning was implanted compared to usual care [0 (0%) vs. 7 (3.8%), p = 0.022]. CONCLUSION: A new nurse-led coordinated transitional bundle of interventions model reduces the composite endpoint of all-cause death and all-cause hospitalization both at 90 and 180 days after a discharge for HF, also in high-risk populations. Such a decrease is driven by a reduction of CV and HF hospitalization. Reduction of all-cause mortality was also observed when the full model including a more exhaustive discharge planning process was implemented. Copyright: © 2023 Alcoberro et al. items.title: Breaking the 30-day barrier: Long-term effectiveness of a nurse-led 7-step transitional intervention program in heart failure.

items.summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $ε$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $ετ$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $ε$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.
items.title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions

items.summary: Algorithm-driven services, including search, recommendation, and advertising, rely on multi-stage model pipelines. While research prioritizes model optimization, post-deployment monitoring focuses on operational reliability. Yet operationally healthy systems may still produce poor-quality results, exposing a gap in existing evaluation and monitoring practices. However, a systematic problem formulation and benchmark for this task remain lacking. To bridge this gap, we formulate System Quality Diagnosis (SQD) for algorithm-driven services, a new task that extends quality evaluation beyond identifying poor outcomes to attributing their causes across system components. Focusing on industrial search, we propose WISE, an agentic framework for end-to-end quality diagnosis that discovers user-facing issues and traces their origins to underlying algorithmic components. To improve diagnostic reliability, we introduce ReTrace for constructing evidence-consistent trajectory supervision and Adaptive Harness-Policy Optimization (AHPO) for failure-guided optimization of the agent harness and model policy. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct WISE-BENCH, a real-world multimodal search benchmark that combines user-facing evidence, internal pipeline traces, and expert diagnosis annotations. Extensive experiments show consistent gains across model scales, with WISE achieving 75.20% end-to-end accuracy on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. In production, WISE supports quality auditing, online quality assurance, and model optimization, reducing diagnosis costs and improving downstream relevance models.
items.title: WISE: An Agentic Framework for Whole-page Multimodal Search Experience Attribution

items.summary: Attracting features toward learned in-distribution (ID) regions is an intuitive strategy for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, but does such attraction improve detection? We investigate this question using class-conditioned Hamiltonian dynamics as a controlled testbed and identify an attraction-ranking mismatch: improving individual class-affinity scores need not improve the relative ordering of ID and OOD samples. Our analysis separates misalignment between the driving field and the detection score from ranking failure that persists even when they are aligned. An exact AUROC decomposition and a local boundary analysis identify relative score changes at the ID-OOD ranking boundary as the source of first-order AUROC change under regularity conditions. Experiments demonstrate that a score-aligned rule can improve performance on a held-out source validation split yet consistently degrade it after transfer, even without a single winning-class change. A separate perturbation study finds that near-boundary relative score changes track the direction of small AUROC changes in the tested settings. Finally, centroid approximation and shared scales connect the zero-step score to a static centroid family that includes the existing CTM detector. Together, these results explain why class attraction is insufficient to justify feature refinement and motivate evaluating its effect on the ranking boundary.
items.title: Attraction-Ranking Mismatch in Out-of-Distribution Detection: Theory and Evidence from Hamiltonian Feature Dynamics

items.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents translate model outputs into consequential actions, turning indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem. Existing defenses constrain tool calls, trajectories, or information flows, but often leave action semantics, state dependencies, and evidence relations implicit, limiting generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicating safe updates. We present \ours{}, a dynamic ontology-guided governance framework. \ours{} grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state to derive deterministic ready, waiting, and forbidden decisions. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation, enabling bounded replanning without expanding the agent's authorization boundary. \ours{} evolves its ontology offline from verified training executions. An offline LLM proposes instance-independent action--state axioms, which are accepted only if they address ontology errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. We evaluate \ours{} on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings. \ours{} achieves a 0\% attack success rate (ASR) across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. These results show that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.
items.title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents

items.summary: Generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP) is a rare chronic inflammatory skin disease that can lead to life-threatening complications and require emergency medical treatment. Recurrent GPP flares are characterized by the sudden onset of widespread erythematous skin rash with sterile pustules, at times associated with fever, chills, general malaise, and other systemic inflammatory manifestations. Systemic complications such as cardiorespiratory failure, infections, and sepsis are potentially life-threatening and can result in an emergency department visit and/or hospitalization. Acute GPP episodes can be difficult to recognize and diagnose. The low incidence of the disease, its relapsing nature, the unpredictability of flare onset, and the lack of standardized diagnostic criteria are major obstacles to achieving rapid recognition and diagnosis in both the emergency department and the hospital setting.There is scarce evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of treatments commonly used for GPP; consequently, there is an unmet need for therapies that specifically target the condition. Our aim is to present a multidisciplinary approach to GPP to achieve a rapid diagnosis ensuring that the patient receives the most appropriate treatment for their pathology. The main recommendation for primary care and emergency physicians is to contact a dermatologist immediately for advice or to refer the patient when GPP or a flare is suspected.
items.title: Generalized pustular psoriasis: practical recommendations for Spanish primary care and emergency physicians.

items.summary: When Studebaker closed its South Bend plant in December 1963, many of its workers lost all or most of their pensions, and the case became the one reformers cited for the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. The figures most often repeated, 2,900 workers who received nothing and about 4,000 who received about 15 percent, go back at least to a hearing of the Senate Special Committee on Aging held at South Bend on 4 June 1971. There Senator Vance Hartke said that "the failure of 2,900 Studebaker workers to receive any pension payment whatsoever is wrong," and that "more than 4,000 other Studebaker employees between the ages of 40 and 59 received only 15 percent" of the pensions due them. A telegram from the UAW's president, Leonard Woodcock, printed in the same hearing, gave the union's count: "Of 11,000 active workers at Studebaker 2900 lost all pension entitlements, and 4500, average age 52, average service 23 years, lost all but 15% of their pension entitlements." Project Scroll Research Note 2026-54, version 1. The note sets out the record quoted, where it is held, what it changes, its limits, and what was searched before calling it new. Web version: projectscroll.com/discoveries/notes/2026-54/ .
items.title: Project Scroll Research Note 2026-54: The Studebaker pension figures of 2,900 and "more than 4,000" traced to the Senate hearing at South Bend of 4 June 1971

items.summary: Volunteer fire brigades rely on fragmented alerting channels and radio plus paper for situational awareness, hindering a shared common operational picture (COP). FireOPS integrates smartphone alerting, navigation, a live geospatial COP, a district resource-load overview and contextual manuals into a human-centric decision-support surface for commanders and responders, running on an edge + cloud architecture whose dual-channel provides source-level redundancy against failure of either the radio or the provincial server feed; delivery to smartphones still depends on the cloud core and mobile networks. This lessons-learned report presents the design rationale, positions FireOPS within emergency-response information systems research, and reports operational findings from a primary log extract of a major regional flood in 2024 and from the 2025 public app release. A feature-matrix comparison with DIVERA 24/7, blaulichtSMS and the LifeRescue prototype identifies COP, decision support and dual-ingestion redundancy as the main differentiators, and we map the operational gaps observed during the flood to concrete engineering responses, deployed or in active development.
items.title: FireOPS: A Human-Centric Emergency Operations Platform

items.summary: Background: The high failure rate of innovation projects motivates us to understand the perceptions about resistances and barriers of the main stakeholders to improving success rates.Objective: This study aims to analyze the readiness for change in the implementation of a 3D printing project in a Catalan tertiary hospital prior to its implementation.Methods: We used a web-based, voluntary, and anonymous survey using the Normalization Measurement Development questionnaire (NoMAD) to gather views and perceptions from a selected group of health care professionals at Germans Trias i Pujol University Hospital. Results: In this study, 58 professionals, including heads of service (n=30, 51%), doctors (n=18, 31%), nurses (n=7, 12%), and support staff (n=3, 5%), responded to the questionnaire. All groups saw the value of the project and were willing to enroll and support it. Respondents reported the highest scores (out of 5) in cognitive participation (mean 4.45, SD 0.04), coherence (mean 3.72, SD 0.13), and reflective monitoring (mean 3.80, SD 0.25). The weakest score was in collective action (mean 3.52, SD 0.12). There were no statistically significant differences in scores among professions in the survey.Conclusions: The 3D printing project implementation should pay attention to preparing, defining, sharing, and supporting the operational work involved in its use and implementation. It should also understand, assess, and communicate the ways in which the new set of practices can affect the users and others around them. We suggest that health officers and politicians consider this experience as a solid ground toward the development of a more efficient health innovation system and as a catalyst for transformation. ©Francesc López Seguí, Joan Cos Codina, Laura Ricou Ríos, María Isabel Martínez Segura, Laura Miró Mezquita, Raquel Escrich Navarro, Meritxell Davins Riu, Oriol Estrada Cuxart, German Anashkin Kachalin, Daniel Moreno-Martínez. Originally published in JMIR Human Factors (https://humanfactors.jmir.org), 06.10.2023.

items.summary: Training an agent to play Pac-Man with only up, down, left and right actions raises a basic question: when performance is poor, what should be improved? Difficulty can arise from reading the screen or from choosing actions over a long sequence. We examine these problems in a Qwen3.5-9B-based agent through separate perception checks and primitive-policy reinforcement-learning studies. In the policy study, which uses textual boards to remove image transcription from the decision interface, completion on eight held-out mazes increased from 0% before this optimization to 80.2% at a selected checkpoint, with three extra lives. The perception checks show that accurate static screenshot reading can coexist with errors during interaction. A separate policy comparison also shows that further optimization can accompany worse action choices. Together, these findings motivate concrete checks for post-training: evaluate perception in use, distinguish training success from full-game validation, and examine decisions and later performance rather than relying on one selected score. The study provides empirical lessons for improving future agent training and evaluation.
items.title: Where It Breaks: Diagnosing Perception, Memory, and Decision Failures of a Vision-Language Agent in Pac-Man

items.summary: Preprint, ChemRxiv, 30.08.2026. Abstract Air quality networks measure pollutant concentrations only at instrumented sites, leaving most locations unobserved. Graph-based virtual-node methods increasingly fill this gap, but are usually summarised by a single leave-one-station-out (LOO) R2 that leaves unstated where the model can be trusted and why it fails. Here, the operating envelope is the object of study. A graph attention network (GAT) combining multi-pollutant lags, ERA5 meteorology, MODIS aerosol optical depth, and land-use composition predicts daily-mean PM10 at unmonitored locations on the 18-station Styrian (Austria) network for 2020–2023. Under LOO cross-validation with disjoint years, the GAT reaches a median R2 of 0.52, seed-stable and ahead of Lagged-IDW (0.26), Lagged-Kriging (0.22), and Ridge-AR (0.45). At two stations whose PM10 distributions lie outside the training support, performance degrades sharply. Ablation and attribution trace the failure to one component: inverse-distanceweighted imputation of held-out lag features interacting with the persistence-residual head; graph topology is immaterial. An outlier-gated imputation policy raises pooled mean R2 from 0.31 to 0.38, node-masking training cuts per-station variance fourfold, and zeroing all auxiliary inputs lifts both outlier stations to positive R2: the partition is induced by the feature pipeline, not the architecture. The partition reproduces on NO2, and the model transfers to the 33-station Bavarian network (median R2 0.39, no negative folds). The outof-scope stations are clean-air sites under-represented in an urban-industrial network, and the worst is flagged in advance by a static-feature outlier detector: a deployable signal of where virtual-node estimates can be trusted and where the network must grow in regime diversity.
items.title: Graph attention networks for daily PM10 prediction at unmonitored European monitoring sites: operational scope, diagnostics, and outlier-robust training

items.summary: Debates about AI and responsibility ask whether automation opens responsibility gaps. This book argues that the more pressing failure lies elsewhere: an institution can remain fully responsible and accountable, yet lose its claim to be relied on, because it issues more than it can answer for. In the book's fictional test case, an insurer's AI appeals agent tells a policyholder: "I have reconsidered my decision. I have reversed it." Nothing happens, because the agent never had the power to reverse anything. The insurer still owns the refusal. No one is off the hook, yet no one answered. Three results Missing bearership is not defective ownership. Answerability is defined as four public relations: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence and standing-consequence. On that account, an AI interface can occupy a role emptily while the institution behind it still owns the role's commitments. So there can be no global responsibility gap and still a genuine local Empty Occupancy. Testimonial force without testimony. Machine output can inform and invite reliance without anyone owning it. Institutions may adopt such output only when five conditions of Normative Sponsorship are met: epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection and repair power. Authority must be serviceable. Because practical authority is defeasible, reliance must remain revisable while a claim operates. Obligations that mature without timely service accumulate as Deontic Debt. Where no credible plan could service issuance at a given scale, the institution is insolvent in a precise sense. It loses presumptive authority, while its duties of ownership and repair survive. Tested against the record and its rivals Robodebt yields a determinate Deontic Debt that case-by-case actor–forum accountability does not settle. The insolvency finding remains provisional, and the book names the records that would decide it. Moffatt v. Air Canada and the DPD chatbot episode leave interface standing indeterminate, and the book says so. TennCare, Post Office Horizon and the Dutch childcare-benefits affair discipline the comparisons. A dedicated chapter engages Bovens, List and Pettit, the responsibility-gap sceptics (Tigard, Königs, Himmelreich) and Lazar. The book closes with explicit conditions under which it would be wrong. Scope. The method is philosophical reconstruction with bounded public-record analysis. The terminology carries no legal consequence, and the equations are uncalibrated. Stipulated cases test whether the criteria discriminate, not how often such cases occur. The role criterion does not settle personhood or moral status. For philosophers of testimony, responsibility and group agency; AI-governance researchers; administrative lawyers; auditors and regulators; and anyone a machine has told that their problem was "resolved." 167 pages. items.summary: Abstract. Two Coulomb fields produce singular three-electron integrals that limited Hylleraas evaluations of lithium fine-structure operators. Two integrations by parts reduce the eight relevant operators to two inverse-square families and previously treated integrals. We give one-dimensional representations for their masters T₂, T₃, and alternative cube–square anchors C₂, C₃; C₃ is expressed in classical polylogarithms of weight at most three. Parity separates decoupled sectors from genuinely three-electron sectors. Exact rational reductions through index sum 32 use twelve sufficient masters at the tested exponent sets. Double screening and Gaussian coordinate integration determine these masters to sixty significant digits. Exact collection of the source functions controls cancellation near equal exponents at four tested separations; equal exponents use a separate exact reduction. Numerical comparisons cover 104 pre-specified recursive members and an independent direct sample of 136 decoupled members through index sum 32. Production-size basis matrix elements of P₄ and one component of P₁ agree by two methods to 41–45 digits. On one Intel Xeon Silver 4410Y machine, both families require 5.85–6.99 CPU hours per exponent set at the stated 64-digit output precision. Uniform error bounds, minimal master sets, and the uncovered lower integrals in some class-2 matrix elements remain open. items.summary: Personalized retrieval-augmented generation requires extracting and applying user preferences from extended interaction histories. This task is challenging because preference evidence is scattered across past conversations and remains bound to specific temporal and situational contexts. Consequently, isolated fragments rarely provide complete support for a response, while preferences expressed under different conditions are easily conflated. To address these limitations, we propose Weaver, a framework that incrementally weaves memory-conditioned retrieval trajectories with compositional preference reasoning for personalized responses. Weaver operates on a Dual-Layer Retrieval and Reasoning Graph that couples an upper Intent Dependency Graph with a lower Memory-Conditioned Retrieval Trajectory Graph. Dependency Information Gap Tracking represents the information needed to answer the current request and its prerequisite dependencies in the upper graph. Memory-Conditioned Incremental Retrieval uses established premises and clues from retrieved conversations to locate missing evidence, recording the resulting retrieval trajectories in the lower graph. Scope-Aware Compositional Reasoning jointly interprets the accumulated evidence to determine which preferences apply to the request. It identifies complementary and alternative support and distinguishes conflicting claims within the same temporal and situational context. These conclusions iteratively update task premises and remaining information gaps, guiding subsequent retrieval to establish a coherent contextual basis for the final response. Experiments on personalized RAG benchmarks, particularly PersonaMem, demonstrate that Weaver outperforms leading baselines in both evidence completeness and answer quality.
items.title: Weaver: Weaving Preference Evidence through Incremental Reasoning for Personalized Retrieval-Augmented Generation

items.summary: Project Genesis defines a scalable, multi-stage Quantum Tetrahedral Hybrid Propulsion System designed to achieve silent, high-efficiency, solid-state flight. This open-source architecture resolves the two critical limitations that have historically restricted atmospheric electrohydrodynamic (EHD) propulsion to lab-bench models: prohibitive energy requirements and extreme atmospheric sensitivity (arcing under high humidity) . The system transitions past brute-force high-voltage scaling by establishing an integrated, multi-physics environmental loop. A first-generation (Gen 1) trial blueprint achieves this through four highly coordinated stages: Mechanical Pre-Compression: An asymmetrical, non-equilateral triangular array of non-bladed Tesla disc packs (featuring lightweight carbon nanofiber skeletons cross-linked with highly electropositive sugarcane bio-waste and casein proteins) pulls in and compresses ambient air without rotational gyroscopic flight roll. Thermodynamic Densification: A micro-dimpled hexagonal honeycomb stator mesh straightens the turbulent rotational air, while structurally embedded Thermoelectric Coolers (TECs) flash-freeze the incoming column. This spikes absolute air density and mass flow rate before the fluid encounters the primary positive ionic corona rings. Closed-Loop Static Scavenging: High-velocity air-shearing through the nano-textured disc gaps triggers a continuous triboelectric exchange, mechanically pre-charging the air mass and lowering downstream high-voltage demands. Residual exhaust kinetic and acoustic energy is safely recycled via an isolated downstream Triboelectric Nanogenerator (TENG) mesh. Absolute Material Containment: The entire framework is micro-sealed in an iron-flake-infused flexible ceramic UV vacuum coat globally embossed with a bio-mimetic dragonfly skin nano-pillar texture to ensure total hydrophobicity and zero skin-friction drag. Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) is completely trapped within the core by a nested, triple-twisted tungsten wire hexagonal Faraday cage embedded with sub-micron diamond dust and backed by flexible silica aerogel firewalls. Flight maneuvering is handled via Differential Fluidic Thrust Vectoring across a 3D tetrahedral diamond drive configuration. Contactless, biaxial (radial-axial) magnetic stator hinges pivot the side wings from high-load VTOL lift modes into low-profile cruise channels that function as an underbelly ram-air trap. When parked on the tarmac, the architecture functions in reverse as a passive, solid-state trickle-charging engine—harvesting static friction from headlines and converting ambient thermal differentials into current, scaling in charging efficiency as the surrounding weather conditions become more extreme.

items.summary: We present a comprehensive analysis of the Wess-Zumino anomaly effective action of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories in components. After reviewing the coset construction of the Wess-Zumino action in the presence of an unbroken subgroup, the gauging of the conformal algebra and the Wess-Zumino effective action for non-supersymmetric conformal field theories with a U(1) symmetry in two and four dimensions, we revisit the superconformal anomalies of $\mathcal{N}=1$ conformal supergravity. Solving the Wess-Zumino consistency conditions we determine both the bosonic and fermionic superconformal anomalies in a two-parameter family of schemes, to quadratic order in the gravitino. Turning on a chiral compensator multiplet and identifying a local super-Poincaré subalgebra of the conformal supergravity algebra without gauge-fixing the coset symmetries, we employ the coset construction and the superconformal anomalies in order to evaluate the Wess-Zumino action for generic $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories coupled to conformal supergravity. By construction, this action reproduces the Weyl, R-symmetry, and S-supersymmetry coset anomalies, but its transformation under the unbroken Poincaré supersymmetry differs from the corresponding anomaly of the conformal supergravity functional. We show that there exists a local functional of the coset-invariant old-minimal fields that, when added to the Wess-Zumino action, results in a generalized Wess-Zumino action that reproduces all anomalies of the conformal supergravity functional. The same local functional enables us to determine the super-Weyl anomalies and the Wess-Zumino action of old-minimal supergravity, providing a component version of the known superspace Wess-Zumino action.
items.title: Anomaly effective actions for 4d $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories

items.summary: This deposit contains the data and the analysis code that reproduce the Methods and Results of a systematic review of polymer-based dental materials incorporating an engineered self-healing mechanism. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework on 26 October 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QCZFY) before formal screening and before any data were extracted. The review separates three contrasts that the literature conflates under the single heading of healing efficiency: C-I, the baseline penalty of the self-healing material in its virgin state against a capsule-free control; C-II, the recovery of the repaired material against the same material in its virgin state; and C-III, the net position of the repaired material against a conventional material without a healing system. The effect measure is the log ratio of means, back-transformed to a ratio and a percentage. Contents. The extraction matrix holds 105 arm-level rows covering four studies and 17 harmonised outcomes, each row linked to the exact formulation of both arms, the source page and the provenance of the value. Four further tables record the full-text eligibility decisions for the 48 assessed reports, the re-screening of the 96 discarded reports against the registered criteria, the characteristics of the studies carrying extracted data, and the register of 16 departures from the registered protocol. The R pipeline recomputes the 89 arm-level contrasts, the three pre-specified contrasts, the efficient-frontier criterion, both manuscript figures and the main and supplementary effect tables. A validation script asserts 21 reported values and halts the pipeline on any mismatch. Reproduction. R 4.4 or later with the metafor package is the only requirement. Running "Rscript run_all.R" from the root of the package regenerates every output in a few seconds and writes a session record alongside them. Limits of these data. Sixty of the 105 rows derive wholly or partly from provisional single-reader readings of figure panels and were not validated by duplicate digitisation; the provenance columns identify them. Five contrasts have a mean of zero in the numerator or the denominator, so the ratio of means is undefined for them. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were not assessed. Arm-level data were extracted from four of the 39 included studies. Licensing. items.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in both producing and evaluating scholarship, raising fundamental questions about how editorial judgments should be documented, contested, and governed. Existing publication models offer complementary approaches to access, selection criteria, review visibility, and preservation, yet these dimensions must be specified independently when evaluative work is delegated to AI systems. This inaugural editorial/perspective introduces the Journal of Autonomous Scholarship (JAS), a fee-free, open- access, multidisciplinary journal welcoming human-authored, AI-assisted, and AI-generated manuscripts under a uniform standard of evidential support, methodological or logical validity, clarity, and research integrity. JAS combines seven explicitly identified AI editorial roles and two revision-continuity auditors with publicly reusable review instructions, hash-bound review provenance, a mechanical and substantive acceptance gate that blocks unresolved material objections, author proof verification, and named human administrative oversight. To support inspection, we assemble a dated companion archive containing local source files, policy and handbook documents, machine-readable prompts and schemas, a synthetic serialization fixture, and extracted historical review reports. The archive is embedded in the supplement PDF; reviewer access does not depend on a separately uploaded ZIP. A file-hash manifest identifies the local snapshot; its equivalence to the previously cited repository commit and the original runtime environment has not been established. We distinguish normative policy requirements, implemented software controls, and prelaunch verification limits, examine risks arising from correlated model errors, non-execution of code during text-based review, and single-publisher governance, and specify a prospective benchmark agenda with finding- and manuscript-level error metrics and cluster-robust uncertainty estimation. items.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.
items.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?

items.summary: Confidence estimates guide human review in LLM-built knowledge graphs, but better error prediction can yield little improvement in an audit. We study this gap through repairability, selection headroom and label validity. Modelling non-adaptive auditing as budgeted covering, we characterise the minimal decision-relevant error statistics and bound the regret of scalar-preserving first-order planning by a structural mass $Δ^{\mathrm{cl}}$. We simulate ideal repair against benchmark-aligned labels for five extraction configurations and two cross-document graphs on Re-DocRED, followed by frozen confirmation on test and replication on 500 hash-selected training documents. On the held-out cross-document graphs, an error-rate $\times$ fan-out queue leaves 3.98-4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint model with the same actions. By comparison, opening shared actions for that joint planner reduces residual errors by 0.89-1.43 points relative to its own fact-only plans, in point estimates. Equivalence between joint and independent-block models remains inconclusive. Generic LLM verification improves three of four model-budget configurations on each held-out set. LLM adjudication identifies possible benchmark omissions.
items.title: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge-Graph Audit?

items.summary: Anonymous nearby tipping has a recognizable cultural form — the "Faith in Humanity Restored" social-media trend in which service workers post videos of unexpected generous tips — but lacks the infrastructure to scale beyond cash. Cash and credit-card payment rails fail at two structural properties that the cultural form requires: tippers cannot be genuinely anonymous to recipients with either rail (cash demands physical hand-over with eye contact; credit-card leaves an identity trail), and recipients cannot prove on social media that an anonymous tip was authentic rather than fabricated (every "Faith in Humanity Restored" video faces a "this is staged for views" credibility problem that erodes the cultural moment). This paper specifies the Thank-All-Nearby primitive — a one-tap operation that broadcasts gratitude, with optional money or time attachment, to every Proof-of-Humanity-verified recipient within Bluetooth Low Energy proximity (or, in institutional-mode deployments, within a GPS bounding-box for institutional locations such as shelters, classrooms, restaurant break-rooms, and worker spaces) — and develops its placement as the operational mechanism for emotional infrastructure for invisible kindness : the restoration of the felt sense of being held in another human's awareness as a property of shared physical space. The primitive composes four prior contributions (PoH℠'s verified-human guarantee, Bluetooth Low Energy plus Apple/Google Nearby framework proximity verification, recipient-side filtering, bilateral uncacheable anonymity) into a single operation whose user-facing surface is one button. The architecture is offered defensively to the commons under CC0. The authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the primitive, its operational specification, the integration with PoH℠, the institutional-mode GPS-bounding-box variant, the recipient-experience design, or any portion thereof. items.summary: In solving systems of nonlinear equations, one of the main objectives is to construct iterative methods that attain high orders of convergence using as few evaluations as possible. However, the information a method obtains during each iteration imposes limitations on the order it can guarantee. The Cordero–Torregrosa conjecture proposes a bound on this order in terms of the number of evaluations of the function and its Jacobian. In this work, we prove this bound for the universal local order of one iteration, without requiring the number of Jacobian evaluations to be less than or equal to the number of function evaluations. In particular, our result also covers the case in which more evaluations of the Jacobian than of the function are performed. The proof encompasses deterministic, causal, memoryless methods whose rules may be arbitrary, without imposing rationality, continuity, or computability conditions. Moreover, we prove that when each Jacobian evaluation is performed at a point where the value of the function is already known, a more restrictive bound on the order of convergence can be obtained. Finally, we propose a new conjecture that establishes a refined bound through a product of factors determined by the distribution of evaluations, under additional dimensional conditions. These results provide a better understanding of the limitations imposed by the available information and raise new possibilities for studying high-order iterative methods.
items.title: Proof of the Cordero–Torregrosa Conjecture and an Improved Order Bound for Paired Jacobian Evaluations

items.summary: The continuous expansion of digital infrastructure, especially data centers, has imposed unprecedented, geographically concentrated stress on existing power grids. However, rigorous causal evidence quantifying how these facilities reshape local power-infrastructure supply remains limited. This study builds a comprehensive county-level US panel dataset spanning 2010-2024, uniquely integrating individual data center building footprints and power-plant additions. To mitigate endogeneity and high-dimensional confounding, this study deploys Double Machine Learning with five-fold cross-fitting, conditioning on county and year fixed effects alongside regional socioeconomic covariates. Baseline estimation identifies a significant positive causal effect robust across multiple rigorous specifications. The result holds following 1%-99% winsorization that downweights mega-clusters including Loudoun County: growth in data-center floor area drives meaningful increases in nearby power-generation capacity (ATE=1.982, P=0.000, CI: [1.25, 2.72]). Outcomes remain statistically significant using a one-year lagged treatment to address reverse causality, and are stable under state-level fixed-effect alternatives. An event-study framework augmented with historical agglomeration controls validates clear parallel trends and detects a sharp causal spike at t = 3, matching typical utility-scale grid-construction lead times. A placebo test further verifies these causal estimates cannot emerge from random chance. Substantial regional heterogeneity emerges: strong positive impacts concentrate in the West, while significant negative displacement-related effects appear within resource-constrained Northeastern counties. These results deliver timely insights for urban planners and energy regulators, stressing the importance of forward-looking grid-capacity investment to support ongoing digital transformation.
items.title: Data Center Agglomeration and Power Infrastructure Capacity in the United States

items.summary: Public comment submitted to DICOM Working Group 32 on Supplement 253: Waveform Compression (Version 09, 2026-09-18), together with the benchmark it rests on. ITU-T T.261 / ISO-IEC 23003-8 ("H.BWC") is evaluated against the codec set of Buccino et al. 2023 (doi:10.1088/1741-2552/acf5a4) on Neuropixels 1.0 recordings at 384 channels and 30 kHz. The lossless results of that paper were reproduced first as a check (912 cells, paired per-recording median deviation 0.017 %, codec ranking 11/11), and T.261 was then added to the same protocol. The central finding is that the two obvious ways to qualify a lossy setting disagree with each other. On one simulated Neuropixels recording with ground truth, at matched compression T.261 preserves the average spike waveform better than WavPack Hybrid while adding six times as many spurious units above the lossless baseline (+30 against +5, on a baseline of 126). A lossy setting therefore cannot be qualified on waveform fidelity alone. The comment makes eight specific requests of WG-32 on that basis, including conveying the quantizer step rather than only a compression ratio, widening Relative Sample Times (which saturates at 71.6 minutes as VR UL), and using a 64-bit Basic Offset Table (32-bit offsets overflow after ~11 minutes of compressed data at 384 channels, and ~2.7 minutes on a 1,536-channel Neuropixels 2.0 Quad Base probe). Every quantitative claim derives from recorded computation rather than from prose: each measurement cell carries its own datalad run record naming the tool commit, input checksums and command line, and each sweep is re-runnable from the pinned tool commit. items.summary: As Generation Z becomes the dominant demographic cohort entering the global labor force, organizational human resource practices face an unprecedented paradigm shift regarding work-life balance and employee retention. This critical review systematically synthesizes recent empirical and theoretical literature (2021–2026) examining the nexus between work-life balance dimensions—including flexible hybrid schedules, digital boundary management, autonomous schedule crafting, and mental health support—and job satisfaction among Gen Z employees. Applying PRISMA 2020 protocol, 16 benchmark studies were critically evaluated. Meta-synthesis indicates that work-life integration significantly enhances job satisfaction and organizational loyalty, primarily mediated by perceived autonomy, reduced burnout, and work-family enrichment. However, hyper-connectivity and blurriness in digital work boundaries introduce novel stressors. The review constructs a structural structural equation modeling (SEM) path framework and formulates a multi-level organizational alignment matrix to optimize Gen Z work-life integration.

items.summary: This paper proposes the Transient-Loss Functional Compounding Theory (TLFCT), a medium-independent, time-indexed framework for investigating how a temporary loss in a system's functional performance may be associated with subsequent capability formation, recovery, net gain, and, under more restrictive conditions, compounding improvement. The central proposition is conditional rather than universal: a transient functional loss can contribute to a positive long-term outcome when a demonstrable conversion mechanism produces retained adaptive capacity or another relevant functional resource, and when the resulting future net benefit is sufficient to offset the initial loss and additional costs. The framework distinguishes transient loss, recovery, compensation, positive net conversion, and functional compounding. It proposes explicit measures for the initial loss, future benefit, subsequent degradation, additional costs, net outcome, loss-to-gain ratio, net conversion index, and break-even time. It also introduces a candidate state-space architecture connecting disturbance, information, feedback, adaptive capacity, performance, and resource constraints. The proposed theoretical architecture contains eighteen analytical layers and nine cross-cutting research modules. Its methodological foundation combines dynamical systems, systems theory, cybernetics, information theory, statistical model selection, and causal inference. A primary case design, a real-time measurement protocol, eight research hypotheses, a falsification strategy, a cross-domain validation plan, and a fourteen-stage research roadmap are specified. TLFCT is presented as a proposed research framework, not as an empirically established universal law. Its mathematical specifications are candidate models whose applicability, identifiability, predictive performance, and domain-level invariance must be established through empirical research.

items.title: The Transient-Loss Functional Compounding Theory (TLFCT)

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.
items.title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application

items.summary: When multi-agent systems act on the external world, a single agent's faulty output can spread across tasks before detection, creating a system-wide blast radius. Single-agent guardrails are confined to individual harnesses, while existing multi-agent controls either cancel only the faulty source and miss downstream consumers or halt and roll back the entire workflow at the cost of healthy work. We present Airlock, a multi-agent runtime and guardrail for selective post-alert fault containment. Its tree-structured runtime, EdgeCitadel, narrows permissions vertically from parent to child agents to establish node boundaries and control switches. Meanwhile, an append-only provenance DAG records cross-agent data consumption horizontally. Upon an alert, Airlock traces forward on this DAG to isolate tainted executions and pending actions, and backward to narrow root causes. At the site switches, a default full quarantine tier freezes affected branches without a solver, while an assured optimized cut tier uses fence-then-prune to enforce a deadline-aware minimum cut minimizing collateral disruption. Across 1,832 testbed runs, 161 physical smart-home LLM runs, and 24,266 simulation records, Airlock blocks all post-alert faulty actuations on our main testbed and smart-home grids with zero post-convergence leaks. Whereas native controls in A2A and LangGraph either contain at most 33.3% of faults or retain at most 16% of work without redo, Airlock retains +68 pp to +96 pp more healthy work, and its optimized cut retains +46 pp more than full quarantine under dense spread. These results show that co-designing runtime authority boundaries with online provenance enables surgical fault containment without sacrificing healthy work (code: https://github.com/EdgeCitadelTeam/EdgeCitadel).
items.title: Airlock: Bounding the Multi-Agent Blast Radius via Selective Online Containment

items.summary: Background The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) strategy to face the challenges of ageing societies. This strategy is focused on person centered care and the assessment intrinsic capacity (IC). Early identification of five domains of IC (cognition, locomotion, vitality, sensory (hearing and vision), and psychological) has been shown to be related with adverse outcomes and can guide actions towards primary prevention and healthy ageing. IC assessment proposed by the WHO ICOPE guidelines is composed by two steps: First, Screening for decreased IC by the ICOPE Screening tool; second, by the reference standard methods. The aim was to assess the performance of diagnostic measures (sensibility, specificity, diagnostic accuracy, and agreement of the ICOPE Screening tool) compared to the reference standard methods in European community-dwelling older adults. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of the baseline of the ongoing VIMCI (Validity of an Instrument to Measure Intrinsic Capacity) cohort study, which was carried out in Primary Care centers and outpatient clinics from 5 rural and urban territories in Catalonia (Spain). Participants were 207 community dwelling persons >= 70-year-old with Barthel >= 90, without dementia or advanced chronic conditions who provided their consent to participate. The 5 IC domains were assessed by the ICOPE Screening tool and the reference methods (SPPB, gait speed, MNA, Snellen chart, audiometry, MMSE, GDS5) during patients' visit. Agreement was assessed with the Gwet AC1 index. Results ICOPE Screening tool sensitivity was higher for cognition (0.889) and ranged between 0.438 and 0.569 for most domains. Specificity ranged from 0.682 to 0.96, diagnostic accuracy from 0.627 to 0.879, Youden index from 0.12 to 0.619, and Gwet AC1 from 0.275 to 0.842. Conclusion The ICOPE screening tool showed fair performance of diagnostic measures; it was helpful to identify those participants with satisfactory IC and showed a modest ability to identify decreased IC in older people with high degree of autonomy.
